title: BJJ Position Dual Template - Bottom + Top (No Hub)
description: Template for simple positions WITH two perspectives but NO variations (Turtle, North-South, etc.). Generates bottom page + top page only.

metadata.title: Turtle Bottom (Defense) | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master turtle defense and escape strategies. Complete guide to protecting yourself in turtle position and returning to guard with 50% success rate.

bottom.overview: Turtle position from the bottom represents a defensive posture where the practitioner is on hands and knees, protecting their back and neck from attacks. While not ideal, turtle can be a temporary defensive position used to recover guard or stand up. The key is minimizing time in turtle while preventing back takes and submissions. (400+ words minimum)
state_invariants: Bottom player on hands and knees with head protected and elbows tight
Top player attempting to break posture and secure hooks or controls
Bottom player working to either return to guard or escape to standing
prerequisites: Strong defensive posture and base maintenance
Awareness of submission threats (crucifix, chokes, etc.)
key_principles: Keep elbows tight to body to prevent arm isolation
Protect neck by keeping chin tucked and hands connected
Maintain strong base to prevent being flattened
Move continuously - turtle is a transitional position, not a resting place
Use sit-through and granby roll mechanics for escape

counter_transitions.trigger: When opponent establishes seatbelt grip, immediately fight the hands
When opponent commits weight forward, sit through to guard

decision_tree.condition: If opponent is attempting back take with hooks
If opponent has seatbelt control but no hooks

actions.technique: Hand Fight and Roll to Guard

common_errors.error: Remaining static in turtle without escaping
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent time to establish back control or submission
common_errors.correction: Move immediately - turtle is temporary, transition to guard or standing

common_errors.error: Reaching out with arms to post
common_errors.consequence: Exposes arms to crucifix and armbar attacks
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows tight to body at all times

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to establish seatbelt without hand fighting
common_errors.correction: Immediately fight hands when opponent attempts seatbelt grip
Only turtle from positions where you can escape (scrambles, guard passing)
Maintain rounded back with strong posture

training_drills.name: Turtle Escape Drill
training_drills.description: Start in turtle, partner applies pressure. Practice sit-throughs and granby rolls to return to guard.

training_drills.name: Hand Fighting from Turtle
training_drills.description: Partner attempts seatbelt control while you defend hands and escape.

training_drills.name: Turtle to Stand Drill
training_drills.description: Practice standing up in base from turtle position while partner tries to keep you down.

optimal_submission_paths.name: Quick escape to guard
optimal_submission_paths.path: Turtle Bottom → Sit-Through → Guard Bottom → Guard Recovery

optimal_submission_paths.name: Defensive stand-up
optimal_submission_paths.path: Turtle Bottom → Base Up → Stand Up → Neutral Standing

optimal_submission_paths.name: Roll to guard
optimal_submission_paths.path: Turtle Bottom → Granby Roll → Guard Bottom → Closed Guard

retention_rate.description: Percentage of time escaping from turtle successfully

advancement_probability.description: Probability of returning to guard or standing

submission_probability.description: Probability of being submitted from turtle

position_metrics.average_time: 10-30 seconds (should be very brief - transitional position)

expert_insights.danaher: Turtle is not a position to maintain - it's a temporary defensive posture used during transitions. The moment you enter turtle, you should already be executing your escape. The sit-through to guard is the most reliable escape as it creates a barrier between you and your opponent while recovering a more favorable defensive position.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, I use turtle strategically for very brief moments during scrambles, but never stay there. The key is having your escape planned before you even enter turtle. I prefer the sit-through because it's quick and doesn't require perfect timing like the granby roll.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: From turtle, the Twister and electric chair setups make this a dangerous position in 10th Planet. But when you're the one in turtle, you need to escape immediately. The granby roll is great if you're flexible, but most people should just sit through to half guard and start working lockdown.

metadata.title: Turtle Top (Attacks) | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master turtle attacks and back takes. Complete guide to breaking turtle position and securing back control with 60% success rate.

top.overview: Attacking the turtle from top position provides numerous opportunities for back takes, submissions, and dominant position advancement. The key is systematically breaking opponent's defensive structure while preventing their escape to guard or standing. Understanding multiple attack paths ensures success against defensive turtles. (400+ words minimum)
state_invariants: Top player positioned over opponent in turtle with control options available
Bottom player in defensive turtle posture attempting to escape
Top player working to establish hooks, controls, or submissions
prerequisites: Ability to break turtle defensive structure
Knowledge of submission opportunities from turtle
key_principles: Prevent opponent from sitting through to guard
Establish seatbelt control as primary objective
Insert hooks systematically once control is secured
Use weight to flatten opponent if they remain static
Attack submissions while advancing to back control

counter_transitions.trigger: When opponent attempts to stand, use mat return to keep them down
If opponent successfully sits through, immediately establish guard passing position
If opponent rolls to back, follow movement and secure mount

decision_tree.condition: If opponent remains static in turtle
If opponent is mobile and attempting escapes
If opponent exposes arm during escape attempt

common_errors.error: Attempting hooks before establishing seatbelt control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes to guard or standing easily
common_errors.correction: Always secure seatbelt first, then systematically insert hooks

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to sit through without following
common_errors.correction: Follow opponent's movement and establish guard passing position

common_errors.error: Using only strength to flatten opponent
common_errors.correction: Use technique and control points rather than pure strength

common_errors.consequence: Opponent stands and resets to neutral
common_errors.correction: Use mat returns and maintain downward pressure
Establish seatbelt and hooks before committing to submissions

optimal_submission_paths.name: Systematic back take
optimal_submission_paths.path: Turtle Top → Seatbelt Control → Insert First Hook → Insert Second Hook → Back Control

optimal_submission_paths.name: Clock choke finish
optimal_submission_paths.path: Turtle Top → Collar Grip → Walk Around → Clock Choke → Won by Submission

optimal_submission_paths.name: Darce from turtle
optimal_submission_paths.path: Turtle Top → Opponent Sits Through → Darce Grip → Roll to Side → Won by Submission

optimal_submission_paths.name: Crucifix path
optimal_submission_paths.path: Turtle Top → Isolate Arm → Crucifix Control → Back Take or Submission

retention_rate.description: Percentage of time maintaining turtle top position

advancement_probability.description: Probability of advancing to back control

submission_probability.description: Probability of finishing directly from turtle

expert_insights.danaher: The turtle position offers exceptional back taking opportunities when approached systematically. The sequence is always the same: establish seatbelt control, secure one hook, then the second hook. Never rush to insert hooks without first controlling the upper body through the seatbelt grip. This prevents the sit-through escape and ensures your back take is controlled and high-percentage.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: I love attacking turtle because most people don't escape properly. They stay static thinking they're safe. The moment someone turtles against me, I'm looking for the seatbelt and hooks. If they try to sit through, I follow to darce or anaconda. The key is being patient with your back take - don't force the hooks, wait for the right moment.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: From turtle top, the Twister system opens up if your opponent is flexible. The Twister and Electric Chair are 10th Planet specialties from this position. But even if you're not going for those, the basic back take principles still apply - secure the seat belt, get your hooks in, and work your submissions from there.
